Air Friction Air drag accounts for an average 5% of combustion engine energy use, with a range from 3% to 12%. Cold temperatures increase the air density and hence air drag. The ideal gas law, PV = nRT, allows one to estimate how the density of air changes under very cold conditions (P = pressure, V = volume, n = number of particles, R = universal gas constant, and T = temperature in Kelvin— i.e., Celsius + 273). The density of air influences the vehicle air drag, and thus the amount of energy required to keep the vehicle moving forward. The density of air is proportional to n/V. From the ideal gas law, n/V is proportional to P/T (times a constant, which does not change). Data were pulled from the Fairbanks International Airport’s METAR notifications to get the pressure and temperature (in Celsius, converted to Kelvin) for both the cold period (Jan. 15–Feb. 4, 2024) and June 2024 time frame.
